 Alaska midterm turnout sets all-time record, beating marijuana-legalization year of 2014
 By 
 James Brooks 
 - 
 November 18, 2026 5:47 pm 
 Voters are seen on the first day of early in-person voting in the midterm elections at a polling site in Juneau on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 More Alaskans voted in this year’s midterm election than any other in state history, according to preliminary figures published Wednesday by the Alaska Division of Elections. 
 Wednesday was the deadline for the division to conduct a ranked choice tabulation and present preliminary results. Final, certified results are expected by Nov. 25.  
 According to Wednesday’s tally, 290,323 Alaskans cast ballots in the primary, beating the prior midterm record of 285,449, set in 2014.  
 That year’s election had a hotly contested U.S. Senate race and three popular ballot measures, including one that legalized marijuana for recreational use in Alaska.  
 KHNS-FM in Haines reported that the village of Klukwan had the highest turnout of any individual precinct: 50 of 70 registered voters in the town cast ballots in the election. 
 In Alaska, voter turnout is higher in presidential election years than in midterm elections. Overall, this year’s participation is the seventh-highest overall: More ballots were cast this year than in the 2000 presidential election or any election before that.  
 An unusual number of ballots were cast before Election Day as well: Only the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections saw a higher proportion of votes cast in advance of Election Day.  
 Alaska’s atypically high voter registration rate means turnout measurements that use percentages are misleadingly low.  
 Alaska had 605,433 people registered to vote for the election. The state has an estimated voting-eligible population of 543,594 people , meaning that the state’s voter registration rate is 111.4%.  
 Federal and state laws make it significantly easier to register to vote than be removed from the state’s voter rolls, and Alaska has a transient population with large numbers of people moving in and out of the state annually.  
 Many people registered to vote in Alaska are members of the military, college students or others who now live in other states but remain registered to vote in Alaska to preserve eligibility for the Permanent Fund dividend and to avoid state income taxes.
